314.1 k km2 against the infobox 315,331 km2 for 2020s Oman (ratio 1.00): the modern outline, which includes Dhofar and Musandam. The Oman page has 'Sultanate of Oman' from 9 August 1970; no page opened gives the border treaties with the UAE, Saudi Arabia or Yemen.
Same shape as 1973 (314.1 k km2, infobox 315,331 km2 for 2020s Oman); Haitham bin Tariq succeeds on the death of Qaboos on 10 January 2020 (Oman page).

ledger.note: 1744: the Persians still hold the coast. Taqi Khan's army besieged Sohar for nine months and then confirmed Ahmad 'as governor of Sohar and Barka in return for tribute'; the Oman page has Persian forces occupying parts of the country 'on two occasions between 1737 and 1744'.

region.text: Rustaq, Nizwa, Sohar and Barka, Muscat still held by the Persians

ledger.note: 20 November 1744: Ahmad bin Said is elected Imam of Oman, founding the Al Bu Said dynasty at Rustaq. 'Ahmad bin Said became the elected Imam of Oman on 20 November 1744'; his election 'marked the end of the Ya'rubid dynasty'. The Ahmad bin Said page instead gives his election as 9 June 1749 at Rustaq (infobox reign 1744-1783).
1747: the Persians are expelled. Ahmad 'invited the remaining Persian troops to a banquet at his fort in Barka'; other historians say they 'voluntarily withdrew on their own accord'.

1747: Muscat and the coast return to Omani rule after the expulsion of the Persians (Cliopatria's Muscat appears in 1748). Disagreement (added by reviewer me-10-c): the Oman page has the Persians occupying parts of the country 'on two occasions between 1737 and 1744' and has them expelled before Ahmad's election of 20 November 1744 ('After the Omanis expelled the Persians'); 1747 rests on the Ahmad bin Said page.

region.text: the Gwadar enclave on the Makran coast

ledger.note: By 1783: Gwadar. 'By 1783, the Omani Empire had expanded eastwards to Gwadar in present-day Pakistan.' The page does not say who held it before.
1792: the capital moves from Rustaq to Muscat (infobox: Rustaq 1692-1792, Muscat 1792-1832).

region.text: the Buraimi Oasis and the part of Oman Saud captured

ledger.note: 1805: the Wahhabis take part of Oman. 'In 1805 Saud managed to capture a part of Oman.' 'The same year he also annexed the Buraimi Oasis.'

region.text: the Omani coast of East Africa, Zanzibar and Mombasa's neighbours

ledger.note: 1814 (Cliopatria's year, page silent): the East African coast becomes its own row (the Omani Slave Coast). No page opened dates the split; the omani-slave-coast dossier gives it as a found event at confidence 1.
1820 (Cliopatria's year, page silent): the oasis returns after the fall of Diriyah in 1818. The Buraimi dispute page calls Hamasa 'one of three Omani villages in the oasis'.
The early 1820s: the Gulf coast is lost. 'In the early 1820s, lost territory in the Persian Gulf, which became the Trucial States under British protection.'
1830 (Cliopatria's year, page silent on a conquest): Dhofar and Salalah. The Dhofar page: 'remained loyal to the sultans of Muscat' in the early 19th century.
1854: the Kuria Muria islands go to Britain. 'In 1854, a deed of cession of the Omani Kuria Muria islands to Britain was signed.'

region.text: Zanzibar and the Omani coast of Africa, to Majid bin Said

ledger.note: 1856: the Omani Empire divides. 'In 1856, under British arbitration, Zanzibar and Muscat became two different sultanates'; Said bin Sultan died on 4 June (the Said page's infobox: 19 October 1856), Thuwaini took the mainland.

1856: the state becomes the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman. 'In 1856, upon the death of the last ruler of the Omani Empire'; Thuwaini bin Said 'ruler of the mainland'. The Oman page infobox gives 8 January 1856 for the name.
1876: Dhofar slips away. Sayyid Fadhl bin Alawi 'had established himself as the de facto ruler of Dhofar', claiming Ottoman allegiance.
January 1879: Dhofar returns. 'He was expelled by local sheikhs in January 1879'; Sayyid Turki then 'established his rule there at the invitation of the Sayyids of Salalah' (undated).

region.text: the interior: Nizwa, Rustaq, north to Ibri, south to Alsharqiyah

ledger.note: 1913: the interior secedes. 'In 1913, Imam Salim ibn Rashid al-Kharusi instigated an anti-Muscat rebellion.'

region.text: the interior around Nizwa and Rustaq

ledger.note: 1913: the rebellion against Muscat begins and runs to 1920.
25 September 1920: the Treaty of Seeb ends the rebellion; it 'resulted in a de facto split between Oman and Muscat'.

region.text: the interior ruled by the Imamate

ledger.note: 25 September 1920: the interior becomes autonomous under the Imamate. The Oman page: the treaty 'granted autonomy to the interior'; the Imamate page: 'The interior part (Oman) was ruled by the Imamate, and the coast (Muscat) by the Sultanate'.
31 August 1952: Saudi guards enter Hamasa. 'a group of some 80 Saudi Arabian guards, 40 of whom were armed' entered Hamasa, 'one of three Omani villages in the oasis'.

1954: the Sultanate attacks the Imamate. 'In 1954, a new imam, Ghalib Alhinai, defended the Imamate from the attacks of the Sultanate of Muscat'; the Muscat and Oman page dates the Jebel Akhdar War to 1954.

region.text: the interior and the Jebel Akhdar

ledger.note: 1954: the Jebel Akhdar War begins (infobox of the Muscat and Oman page; the Imamate page gives only the end).

25 October 1955: the oasis is retaken. 'the British government decided to unilaterally abrogate the Standstill Agreement and take the oasis on 25 October 1955'; the Trucial Oman Levies captured the Saudi contingent. Britain later split the oasis, 'ceding the areas under the Na'im and Al Bu Shamis, Buraimi and Hamasah, to Oman'.
8 September 1958: Gwadar is sold. 'On 8 September 1958, Pakistan purchased the Gwadar enclave from Oman for US$3 million.'
1959: the Jebel Akhdar War ends ('lasted until 1959') with the Sultan victorious 'with direct British support'.
1959: the interior comes under direct rule again after the Imamate's defeat; the page gives no date for the end of its autonomy beyond the war.

1963: the Dhofar War begins. The Dhofar page titles it the 'Omani Civil War (1963-76)'; the Sultan's forces fought the Dhofar Liberation Front, then the Marxist PFLOAG, backed by South Yemen; the Muscat and Oman page dates the Dhofar Rebellion to 1962.
1967: the Kuria Muria islands come back. 'the sultanate did gain some territory in 1967, when Britain returned the Khuriya Muriya Islands.'
9 August 1970: Qaboos proclaims the Sultanate of Oman. Said bin Taimur was 'deposed in a bloodless coup in 1970 by his son Qaboos bin Said' (23 July 1970, Muscat and Oman page).
December 1975: 'once the campaign was declared over in December 1975', the remaining PFLOAG fighters surrendered (the Oman page: 'finally put down in 1976').

wars.name: Persian invasion of Oman
wars.outcome: Persian forces hold Muscat and besiege Sohar; Ahmad bin Said serves as tributary governor of Sohar and Barka and drives the Persians out in 1747.
wars.note: Oman page: Persians 'occupied parts of the country on two occasions between 1737 and 1744'; Omani Empire page: 'Persian invasion of Sohar: 1742'. The Ya'rubid civil war ran from 1718 to the death of Bal'arab in 1749.

wars.name: Wahhabi conquest of Buraimi

zones.text: the Buraimi Oasis and the part of Oman Saud captured

wars.outcome: The Wahhabis hold Buraimi from 1805 to the fall of Diriyah (1818).
wars.note: Sultan bin Ahmad died in 1804 (Omani Empire page); Badr bin Saif, 'allied with the Wahhabis', was murdered by Said bin Sultan in 1806 (Omani Empire page).

wars.name: Imamate of Oman rebellion
wars.outcome: Treaty of Seeb, 25 September 1920: a de facto split, the interior autonomous under the Imamate.
wars.note: The page does not give a battle record.

wars.name: Buraimi dispute

zones.text: the Buraimi Oasis, Al Ain and Hamasa

wars.outcome: Saudi guards occupy Hamasa from 31 August 1952; the British take the oasis on 25 October 1955; Britain splits it, Buraimi and Hamasa to Oman, Al Ain to Abu Dhabi; the 1974 Treaty of Jeddah settles the dispute.
wars.note: Abu Dhabi and the Trucial States were the other claimant; the Sultan and the Imam were persuaded by Britain to hold back.

wars.name: Jebel Akhdar War

zones.text: the interior and the Jebel Akhdar

wars.outcome: The Sultan, with direct British support, defeats the Imamate in 1959.
wars.note: The Imamate page gives only 'lasted until 1959'; the Muscat and Oman infobox gives 1954.

wars.name: Dhofar War
wars.outcome: The Sultan's forces, helped by the United Kingdom, Iran, Pakistan and India, defeat the rebels, declared over in December 1975.
wars.note: Titled 'Omani Civil War (1963-76)' on the Dhofar page; the Muscat and Oman page dates the rebellion from 1962.

certainty.note: Coastal towns, oases and tribal lands; the interior was autonomous 1920-1954; the Gwadar enclave and the Kuria Muria islands are exact (sale of 8 September 1958; cession of 1854).

Cliopatria's modern outline (314,076 km2 against the infobox 315,331 km2); no page opened gives the dates of the border treaties with the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Yemen, and the Buraimi settlement is the Treaty of Jeddah of 1974.

notes: Page budget (9 pages) spent on Oman, Ahmad bin Said, Said bin Sultan, Omani Empire, Muscat and Oman, Dhofar, Fort Jesus, Imamate of Oman and Buraimi dispute; the Saud bin Abdulaziz bin Muhammad page belongs to the Diriyah dossier. MERGE: Cliopatria splits the Al Bu Said sultanate in two rows, 'Sultanate of Oman' (1744-1899, 1973-2024) and 'Sultanate of Muscat and Oman' (1900-1946), with no shape for 1947-1972; the Muscat and Oman page and the Imamate page treat them as one state ('Muscat and Oman' dates from 1856 and became the Sultanate of Oman in 1970), so this dossier reviews both rows (cliopatria_names) and adds new keyframes for 1947-1972. The sultanate-of-muscat-and-oman dossier of another part of group me-10 should be dropped as an alias, or this one split; the colours.json assigns them different colours. Cliopatria rows: 1744-1812 shapes include Mombasa (not Omani 1741-1837); Gwadar (Omani 1783-1958) is in no shape; 1900-1921 shapes carry Kuwait and Qatar cells; Muscat's cell is missing from 1920-1946; Dhofar is missing 1898-1921. Not settled: the 1757 growth to the Trucial coast and its loss (Sharjah 1800, Fujayrah 1811, Sohar and Musandam 1811), the four Iranian-coast cells of 1811-1869, the Wahhabi hold of 'Bahrain and Oman' (undated), who held Gwadar before 1783, who held Dhofar in 1856-1875, and the end of the interior's autonomy (1954 war start; 1959 end). British protection (1891-1970, 'De facto British protected state') belongs to the kingdom-of-great-britain dossier as a vassal event with counterpart sultanate-of-oman. Counterparts needing dossiers: the Dhofar Liberation Front/PFLOAG (type rebel, Dhofar 1963-1975, suggested slug pfloag), Fadhl bin Alawi's Dhofar (1876-1879, minor), the Emirate of Abu Dhabi (Buraimi). Gazetteer names missing: none for Oman proper; Kuria Muria is drawn as a radius at 17.5 N 56.0 E. Capitals: the Zanzibar seat of 1832-1856 is the omani-slave-coast dossier's. Sultans are not listed as no complete list was on the pages.
